sql-advanced:0.code:
SELECT e.name
FROM employees e
WHERE e.salary > (
  SELECT AVG(x.salary)
  FROM employees x
  WHERE x.dept_id = e.dept_id
);
options: Employees earning more than the company-wide average
Employees earning more than the average of their own department
Departments whose average salary exceeds the company average
The highest-paid employee in each department
sql-advanced:0.explanation: The inner query references e.dept_id from the outer row, so it is correlated: it computes the average for that employee's department. Without the x.dept_id = e.dept_id condition it would be the company-wide average.

sql-advanced:0.prompt: In PostgreSQL, SELECT name, (SELECT city FROM addresses a WHERE a.user_id = u.id) FROM users u fails for some users with "more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression". What is the cause?
options: Correlated subqueries are not allowed in the SELECT list
Some users have several addresses, and a scalar subquery must return at most one row
users and addresses need a foreign key for the subquery to work
The subquery must use EXISTS when it appears in the SELECT list
sql-advanced:0.explanation: A scalar subquery must return zero or one row (zero gives NULL). Users with several addresses produce several rows. Add a rule to pick one (ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1, or an aggregate) or use a join. Correlated subqueries are allowed in the SELECT list.

sql-advanced:0.prompt: A colleague changes WHERE EXISTS (SELECT * FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) to EXISTS (SELECT 1 ...). What changes?
options: The SELECT 1 version is much faster because it reads fewer columns
Nothing: EXISTS only checks whether any row exists and ignores the select list
SELECT 1 returns true even when there are no matching orders
SELECT * may return duplicate customers, while SELECT 1 does not
sql-advanced:0.explanation: EXISTS stops at the first matching row and never evaluates its select list, so SELECT *, SELECT 1 or SELECT NULL behave identically. SELECT 1 is just a readability convention. EXISTS never duplicates outer rows either way.

sql-advanced:0.prompt: In PostgreSQL, what does LATERAL make possible in this query?
sql-advanced:0.code:
SELECT c.id, o.id AS order_id, o.created_at
FROM customers c
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT id, created_at FROM orders o
  WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
  ORDER BY created_at DESC
  LIMIT 3
) o;
options: It lets the subquery in FROM reference c, so the LIMIT 3 is applied per customer
It makes the subquery run once and caches the result for every customer
It turns the CROSS JOIN into a LEFT JOIN automatically
It is required whenever a subquery in FROM uses ORDER BY
sql-advanced:0.explanation: Without LATERAL, a FROM subquery cannot see columns of earlier FROM items. LATERAL makes it run per outer row, which gives "top 3 orders per customer". CROSS JOIN LATERAL drops customers with no orders; use LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true to keep them.

sql-advanced:0.prompt: Department 10 has no employees. In PostgreSQL, what does this query return?
options: No rows, because there is nothing to compare against
Every employee with a non-NULL salary
An error: ALL requires a non-empty subquery
Only employees who earn more than the global maximum
sql-advanced:0.explanation: x > ALL (empty set) is vacuously TRUE, so every row with a non-NULL salary passes. Rewriting it as salary > (SELECT MAX(salary) ...) would return no rows instead, because MAX of nothing is NULL. The two forms differ exactly on empty input.

sql-advanced:0.prompt: This query takes minutes on 50k customers and 5M orders, and orders.customer_id has no index. Why is it slow?
options: COUNT(*) always scans the whole table in PostgreSQL
The correlated subquery runs once per customer, and without an index each run scans orders: about 50k x 5M row visits
Scalar subqueries disable parallel query, so the plan is single-threaded
The subquery result is not cached, so the customers table is rescanned each time
sql-advanced:0.explanation: Each customer triggers a new execution of the subquery, and with no index each one is a sequential scan of orders. Index orders(customer_id), or rewrite as a GROUP BY over orders joined to customers so orders is read once.

options: The average number of orders across all customers, including those with zero orders
The average number of orders per customer, among customers who have at least one order
The total number of orders divided by the number of distinct order ids
The average order amount per customer
sql-advanced:0.explanation: The derived table only has rows for customer_ids present in orders, so customers with zero orders are not in the average. To include them, LEFT JOIN customers to the counts and use COALESCE(cnt, 0).

sql-advanced:0.prompt: Which predicates return the same customers as WHERE c.id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)? Select all that apply.
options: WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)
WHERE c.id = ANY (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)
An INNER JOIN to orders without DISTINCT
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)
sql-advanced:0.explanation: IN (subquery) is the same as = ANY (subquery), and both are semi-joins equivalent to EXISTS. An inner join repeats customers once per order, and NOT EXISTS returns the opposite set.

sql-advanced:0.prompt: Which statements about correlated subqueries are true? Select all that apply.
options: Logically they are evaluated once per outer row, though PostgreSQL may rewrite them as joins
They can appear in the SELECT list, WHERE and HAVING
They can only be used with EXISTS or IN
They can be copied out and run standalone for debugging without changes
sql-advanced:0.explanation: A correlated subquery references outer columns, so its meaning is per outer row; the planner can still convert EXISTS/IN forms into semi-joins. Because it references outer columns, it does not run on its own until you substitute a value.

sql-advanced:0.prompt: If the subquery in WHERE x IN (SELECT ...) returns the same value several times, the matching outer rows appear several times in the result.
options: True
False
sql-advanced:0.explanation: IN is a membership test (a semi-join), so each outer row is returned at most once no matter how many times its value appears. Duplication happens with a plain JOIN, not with IN or EXISTS.

sql-advanced:0.prompt: A scalar subquery that returns no rows evaluates to NULL instead of raising an error.
options: True
False
sql-advanced:0.explanation: Zero rows give NULL; more than one row raises an error. That is why a SELECT-list lookup such as (SELECT name FROM ... WHERE id = ...) shows NULL for missing matches.

sql-advanced:1.prompt: What is the main benefit of a non-recursive CTE (WITH active AS (...) SELECT ...) over the same SQL written as nested subqueries?
options: It always caches the result, so the query runs faster
It names an intermediate result so the query reads top-down and the name can be reused within the statement
It persists the result across statements in the same session
It is the only way to join a table to itself
sql-advanced:1.explanation: A CTE is a named subquery scoped to one statement, which improves readability and avoids repetition. It is not stored across statements (use a temp table or view for that), and since PostgreSQL 12 it is not necessarily materialized.

sql-advanced:1.prompt: After upgrading from PostgreSQL 11 to 16, a query of the form WITH recent AS (SELECT * FROM events) SELECT * FROM recent WHERE user_id = 42 becomes much faster. Why?
options: PostgreSQL 16 caches CTE results between executions
Since PostgreSQL 12, a side-effect-free CTE referenced once is inlined, so the user_id filter is pushed down and can use an index
PostgreSQL 16 runs every CTE in parallel automatically
PostgreSQL 16 creates a temporary index on CTE output
sql-advanced:1.explanation: Before 12, every CTE was an optimization fence: events was fully materialized and then filtered. Since 12 such a CTE is inlined like a subquery, so the predicate reaches the base table. There is no caching between executions.

sql-advanced:1.prompt: In PostgreSQL 16, which non-recursive, side-effect-free CTE is materialized by default rather than inlined?
options: A CTE referenced once in the main query
A CTE referenced twice in the main query
A CTE referenced once and filtered by the outer WHERE
A CTE referenced once and joined to another table
sql-advanced:1.explanation: PostgreSQL inlines a CTE only when it is non-recursive, has no side effects and is referenced exactly once. Referencing it twice makes it materialize once and reuse the result. You can override either default with MATERIALIZED or NOT MATERIALIZED.

sql-advanced:1.prompt: What makes a WITH RECURSIVE query stop?
options: It stops after a fixed depth configured by max_recursion_depth
It stops when an iteration of the recursive term produces no new rows
It stops when the anchor term returns NULL
It stops after the outer query's LIMIT is reached, every time
sql-advanced:1.explanation: PostgreSQL runs the anchor once, then keeps feeding the latest rows into the recursive term until an iteration returns nothing. There is no built-in depth limit, so a cycle in the data means it never ends unless you guard against it.

sql-advanced:1.prompt: A recursive CTE walks a follows(follower, followee) graph and carries a depth column. The graph has cycles and the query never finishes. A teammate swaps UNION ALL for UNION, and it still never finishes. Why?
options: UNION is not allowed in recursive CTEs, so PostgreSQL ignores it
Each row includes an increasing depth, so revisited nodes are never exact duplicates and UNION removes nothing
UNION only removes duplicates from the anchor term
UNION de-duplicates only after the recursion finishes
sql-advanced:1.explanation: UNION discards rows identical to ones already produced, but (node, depth+1) always differs from (node, depth). Track the visited path (an array plus NOT node = ANY(path)), use the CYCLE clause (PostgreSQL 14+), or cap the depth.

sql-advanced:1.code:
WITH RECURSIVE sub AS (
  SELECT id, manager_id, 1 AS depth
  FROM employees WHERE id = 7
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.manager_id, s.depth + 1
  FROM employees e
  JOIN sub s ON e.manager_id = s.id
)
SELECT * FROM sub;
options: Only employee 7's direct reports
Employee 7 and its chain of managers up to the CEO
Employee 7 plus all direct and indirect reports, each with its depth below 7
An infinite loop, because sub references itself
sql-advanced:1.explanation: The anchor selects employee 7 (depth 1). Each iteration finds employees whose manager is in the previous level, going down the tree. Walking up to the managers would need the join reversed: e.id = s.manager_id.

sql-advanced:1.prompt: What does this PostgreSQL query return?
options: It never terminates
sql-advanced:1.explanation: The CTE produces 1, 2, 3, 4, 5: the iteration from x = 5 adds nothing because WHERE x < 5 fails. 1+2+3+4+5 = 15. Answering 21 assumes 6 is also produced.

sql-advanced:1.prompt: In PostgreSQL, consider WITH moved AS (DELETE FROM jobs WHERE done RETURNING *) INSERT INTO jobs_archive SELECT * FROM moved. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: The delete and the insert happen atomically as one statement
RETURNING is how the deleted rows reach the main query
A SELECT from jobs in the main query would already see those rows gone
A data-modifying CTE runs to completion even if the main query does not read its output
sql-advanced:1.explanation: All parts share one snapshot and commit together, and RETURNING passes rows along. Because of that shared snapshot, the main query does not see the CTE's changes to jobs. PostgreSQL runs data-modifying CTEs exactly once whether or not they are referenced.

sql-advanced:1.prompt: Which statements about WITH RECURSIVE in PostgreSQL are true? Select all that apply.
options: The anchor and recursive terms are combined with UNION or UNION ALL
Each iteration of the recursive term only sees the rows produced by the previous iteration
The recursive term may apply aggregates such as COUNT(*) over the CTE
Each iteration of the recursive term sees every row accumulated so far
sql-advanced:1.explanation: Recursion works on a working table holding only the previous iteration's rows. Aggregates are not allowed in the recursive term (PostgreSQL raises an error), so aggregate in the outer query instead.

sql-advanced:1.prompt: In PostgreSQL 16, every non-recursive CTE is materialized and acts as an optimization fence.
options: True
False
sql-advanced:1.explanation: That was true up to PostgreSQL 11. Since 12, side-effect-free CTEs referenced once are inlined by default; add AS MATERIALIZED to get the fence back.

sql-advanced:1.prompt: In a recursive CTE, the anchor (non-recursive) term is executed only once.
options: True
False
sql-advanced:1.explanation: The anchor seeds the working table once; only the recursive term repeats. Expensive setup therefore belongs in the anchor, not the recursive term.

sql-advanced:2.prompt: Salaries ordered DESC are 100, 90, 90, 80. What do RANK() and DENSE_RANK() assign to the 80?
options: RANK 4, DENSE_RANK 3
RANK 3, DENSE_RANK 3
RANK 4, DENSE_RANK 4
RANK 3, DENSE_RANK 4
sql-advanced:2.explanation: RANK leaves a gap after ties (1, 2, 2, 4), while DENSE_RANK does not (1, 2, 2, 3). ROW_NUMBER would give 1, 2, 3, 4 with an arbitrary order between the two 90s.

sql-advanced:2.prompt: daily_sales(day, amount) has one row per day. Which expression gives the change from the previous day?
options: amount - LEAD(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day)
amount - LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day)
amount - FIRST_VALUE(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day)
amount - SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day)
sql-advanced:2.explanation: LAG reads the value from the previous row in window order; the first day gets NULL. LEAD reads the next row, so it would give the change to the following day.

sql-advanced:2.prompt: Rows are (day 1, 10), (day 2, 5), (day 2, 5). What does SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day) return for the first day-2 row?
options: It varies between runs
sql-advanced:2.explanation: With ORDER BY, the default frame is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, which includes all peers with the same day. Both day-2 rows get 20. Use ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW (with a tiebreaker) for row-by-row totals.

sql-advanced:2.prompt: Why does PostgreSQL reject WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY created_at DESC) = 1?
options: ROW_NUMBER needs an explicit frame clause
Window functions are computed after WHERE, so they cannot be used there; filter in an outer query or CTE
PARTITION BY cannot be combined with ORDER BY in WHERE
ROW_NUMBER returns bigint, which cannot be compared with 1
sql-advanced:2.explanation: Window functions run after FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING, so WHERE cannot see their results. Compute rn in a subquery or CTE and filter WHERE rn = 1 outside. The bigint type is not an issue.

sql-advanced:2.prompt: What is the key difference between AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id) and AVG(salary) ... GROUP BY dept_id?
options: The window version keeps every employee row and attaches the department average to each
The window version is always faster
GROUP BY includes NULL salaries in the average, but the window version does not
PARTITION BY sorts the result by dept_id, while GROUP BY does not
sql-advanced:2.explanation: GROUP BY collapses each department to one row; a window function computes over the partition but keeps the input rows. That lets you compare each salary with its department average. Both ignore NULLs the same way.

sql-advanced:2.prompt: LAST_VALUE(price) OVER (PARTITION BY sku ORDER BY changed_at) returns each row's own price instead of the latest price for the SKU. Why?
options: LAST_VALUE ignores the ORDER BY
The default frame ends at the current row, so the last value in the frame is the current row; add ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
LAST_VALUE only works without PARTITION BY
Rows must be sorted DESC for LAST_VALUE to work
sql-advanced:2.explanation: With ORDER BY, the frame runs from the partition start to the current row (and its peers), so LAST_VALUE sees only up to the current row. Extend the frame to the end of the partition, or use FIRST_VALUE with ORDER BY changed_at DESC.

sql-advanced:2.prompt: daily_metrics(day date, v) has gaps (some days missing). Which frame gives a true 7-calendar-day moving average in PostgreSQL?
options: AVG(v) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
AVG(v) OVER (ORDER BY day RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '6 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
AVG(v) OVER (PARTITION BY day ROWS 6 PRECEDING)
AVG(v) OVER (ORDER BY day GROUPS BETWEEN 7 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
sql-advanced:2.explanation: ROWS counts physical rows, so with gaps the 7 rows can span more than 7 days. RANGE with an interval offset (PostgreSQL 11+) is based on the day value itself. PARTITION BY day puts each day in its own partition.

sql-advanced:2.prompt: Which statements about window functions in PostgreSQL are true? Select all that apply.
options: NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY score) splits the rows into 4 roughly equal buckets
LEAD(x, 1, 0) OVER (ORDER BY t) returns 0 for the last row instead of NULL
Window functions are evaluated after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING
ROW_NUMBER() OVER () with no ORDER BY gives a stable numbering across runs
sql-advanced:2.explanation: NTILE buckets rows, and the third LEAD/LAG argument is the default when no row exists at that offset. Window functions run after grouping. Without ORDER BY, row numbering follows whatever order rows arrive in, which is not guaranteed to be stable.

sql-advanced:2.prompt: You need exactly one row per department, even when salaries tie. Which approaches guarantee that? Select all that apply.
options: Filter ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) = 1
Filter RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) = 1
SELECT DISTINCT ON (dept_id) ... ORDER BY dept_id, salary DESC
Filter DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) = 1
sql-advanced:2.explanation: ROW_NUMBER and DISTINCT ON always keep one row per group (add a tiebreaker to make the choice deterministic). RANK and DENSE_RANK both give tied top earners rank 1, so they can return several rows per department.

sql-advanced:2.prompt: A query can define a named window with a WINDOW clause, e.g. WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary), and reuse it as OVER w in several functions.
options: True
False
sql-advanced:2.explanation: The WINDOW clause avoids repeating identical OVER specifications, and PostgreSQL can compute functions that share a window in one pass over the sorted data.

sql-advanced:2.prompt: Window functions can be nested directly, e.g. SUM(ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id)) OVER ().
options: True
False
sql-advanced:2.explanation: PostgreSQL raises "window function calls cannot be nested". Compute the inner window function in a subquery or CTE, then apply the outer one to its result.

sql-advanced:3.prompt: What does CREATE VIEW active_users AS SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE active store in PostgreSQL?
options: A copy of the matching rows, refreshed nightly
Only the query definition; each query against the view runs it on the current data
An index on users(active)
A cached result that is invalidated when users changes
sql-advanced:3.explanation: A plain view is a saved query that the rewriter expands into each statement that uses it, so it always reflects current data. Storing results is what a materialized view does.

sql-advanced:3.prompt: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY sales_summary fails in PostgreSQL. What is the most likely missing piece?
options: A primary key on the base table
A unique index on the materialized view covering all rows
The view must be created WITH NO DATA first
autovacuum must be disabled during the refresh
sql-advanced:3.explanation: A concurrent refresh diffs old and new contents row by row, which needs a unique index on the materialized view (plain columns, no WHERE clause). Base-table keys are irrelevant, and a view that has never been populated cannot be refreshed concurrently.

sql-advanced:3.prompt: An analytics dashboard runs a 12-second aggregate over 200M rows. Product says data up to 15 minutes old is fine. What is the simplest good fit in PostgreSQL?
options: A plain view over the aggregate
A materialized view with a unique index, refreshed CONCURRENTLY every 15 minutes by a scheduled job
A trigger on the fact table that recomputes the full aggregate on every insert
Increasing work_mem until the query finishes in under a second
sql-advanced:3.explanation: Staleness is acceptable, so precomputing the result and refreshing it on a schedule is cheap and simple. A plain view still runs the 12-second query each time, and a full recompute per insert would cripple writes.

sql-advanced:3.prompt: Every night at 02:00 dashboard queries hang for about 90 seconds and then recover. A job runs REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW sales_summary at 02:00. What is happening?
options: The refresh rebuilds the base table's indexes
A non-concurrent refresh takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on the view, blocking reads until it finishes
The refresh flushes shared_buffers, so every query reads from disk
Materialized views cannot be read while autovacuum runs on them
sql-advanced:3.explanation: A plain REFRESH swaps contents under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, so SELECTs on the view wait. CONCURRENTLY allows reads during the refresh, at the cost of a slower refresh and the need for a unique index.

sql-advanced:3.prompt: Which of these PostgreSQL views is automatically updatable (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE work without triggers)?
options: CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE active
CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id
CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT DISTINCT country FROM users
CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT u.id, o.total FROM users u JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
sql-advanced:3.explanation: PostgreSQL auto-updates simple views: a single base table in FROM, no aggregates, DISTINCT, GROUP BY, set operations or LIMIT. Grouped, DISTINCT and join views need INSTEAD OF triggers or rules.

sql-advanced:3.prompt: Through the view active_users (SELECT * FROM users WHERE active), you run INSERT ... VALUES (..., active = false). The view was created WITH CHECK OPTION. What happens?
options: The row is inserted and immediately disappears from the view
The insert is rejected because the new row would not be visible through the view
The row is inserted with active forced to true
The insert succeeds but only into the view, not into users
sql-advanced:3.explanation: WITH CHECK OPTION makes INSERT/UPDATE through the view fail if the resulting row would not satisfy the view's WHERE. Without it, the insert succeeds and the row silently vanishes from the view. Views store nothing, so writes always go to the base table.

sql-advanced:3.prompt: Role reporting has SELECT on the view customer_public but no privileges on the customers table. Querying the view works. Why, in PostgreSQL 16 defaults?
options: Views bypass all permission checks
Base tables are accessed with the view owner's privileges unless the view is created with security_invoker
SELECT on a view implicitly grants SELECT on its tables
The reporting role inherits privileges from PUBLIC on every table
sql-advanced:3.explanation: By default, a view checks base-table privileges as its owner, which makes views useful for exposing only some columns. PostgreSQL 15 added security_invoker = true to check as the querying user. No grant on the table is implied.

sql-advanced:3.prompt: Which statements comparing PostgreSQL views and materialized views are true? Select all that apply.
options: A materialized view stores its result physically
You can create indexes on a materialized view
You can create an index directly on a plain view
Querying a plain view always reflects the latest committed data visible to your snapshot
sql-advanced:3.explanation: Materialized views are real storage, so they can be indexed and can go stale. Plain views store no rows, so there is nothing to index (index the base tables), and they always read current data.

sql-advanced:3.prompt: Which are workable ways to keep a precomputed summary fresh in PostgreSQL 16? Select all that apply.
options: Scheduled REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY from a cron job
A summary table maintained incrementally by triggers or by the application in the same transaction
Relying on PostgreSQL's built-in incremental maintenance of materialized views
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW ... WHERE updated_at > last_run to refresh only changed rows
sql-advanced:3.explanation: Core PostgreSQL has no incremental view maintenance and no partial REFRESH syntax; every refresh recomputes the whole query. For fresher data, maintain a summary table yourself, or refresh on a schedule.

sql-advanced:3.prompt: In PostgreSQL, DROP TABLE on a table that a view depends on fails unless you add CASCADE.
options: True
False
sql-advanced:3.explanation: PostgreSQL tracks dependencies, so dropping the table errors with "other objects depend on it". CASCADE drops the dependent views too, which is why it should be used with care in migrations.

sql-advanced:3.prompt: Querying a plain view is inherently slower than writing the same query inline, because the view's full result is computed first and then filtered.
options: True
False
sql-advanced:3.explanation: PostgreSQL expands the view definition into the outer query before planning, so outer filters can be pushed down just as with the inline SQL. Materializing first is how materialized views behave, not plain views.

sql-advanced:4.prompt: In PostgreSQL, what can a PROCEDURE (invoked with CALL) do that a FUNCTION cannot?
options: Return a result set
Issue COMMIT or ROLLBACK inside its body to control transactions
Accept parameters
Be written in PL/pgSQL
sql-advanced:4.explanation: Since PostgreSQL 11, procedures can commit and roll back mid-body (when called outside an explicit transaction block), which is useful for batched maintenance. Functions always run inside the caller's transaction. Both accept parameters and can be PL/pgSQL.

sql-advanced:4.prompt: In PostgreSQL, you want INSERTs into a view that joins customers and addresses to write to both tables. What feature is designed for this?
options: A BEFORE INSERT row trigger on the view
An INSTEAD OF INSERT trigger on the view
An AFTER INSERT statement trigger on customers
WITH CHECK OPTION on the view
sql-advanced:4.explanation: Join views are not automatically updatable; INSTEAD OF row triggers on a view replace the INSERT with your own logic that writes to the base tables. BEFORE/AFTER row triggers apply to tables, and CHECK OPTION only validates rows.

sql-advanced:4.prompt: A BEFORE INSERT FOR EACH ROW trigger function on orders returns NULL for some rows. What happens to those rows?
options: They are inserted with all columns NULL
Their insert is silently skipped, with no error
The whole statement fails with an error
They are inserted unchanged, because the return value is ignored
sql-advanced:4.explanation: Returning NULL from a BEFORE row trigger cancels the operation for that row without raising an error, so rows go missing silently. Return NEW to proceed, or RAISE EXCEPTION to fail loudly. The return value of AFTER row triggers is ignored.

sql-advanced:4.prompt: A team debates putting a discount rule in a PostgreSQL trigger versus the Node service. What is the strongest argument for the service?
options: Triggers cannot read other tables
The rule changes often and needs unit tests, code review and visibility next to the rest of the domain logic; triggers are hidden side effects
Triggers always make inserts at least 10x slower
PostgreSQL triggers cannot be versioned in migrations
sql-advanced:4.explanation: Frequently changing business logic is easier to test, debug and deploy in application code, while a trigger runs invisibly on every write. Triggers can read other tables and can be versioned in migrations; the cost is maintainability, not capability.

sql-advanced:4.prompt: Which of these is the most defensible use of a database trigger?
options: Calling a payment provider's HTTP API when an order is inserted
Writing an audit row in the same transaction as every change to a sensitive table
Recomputing a recommendation model whenever a product is viewed
Sending a welcome email when a user row is inserted
sql-advanced:4.explanation: An audit row written by a trigger is atomic with the change and cannot be skipped by any client, including ad-hoc SQL. External calls and emails do not belong in triggers: they cannot be rolled back and they slow every write.

sql-advanced:4.prompt: An AFTER INSERT trigger calls pg_notify('orders', ...), and a Node listener sends a confirmation email. The inserting transaction later rolls back. Is the email sent?
options: Yes, NOTIFY is delivered as soon as pg_notify runs
No, notifications are delivered only when the transaction commits
Yes, but only if the listener is on the same connection
It depends on whether synchronous_commit is on
sql-advanced:4.explanation: PostgreSQL queues NOTIFY and delivers it at commit; on rollback it is discarded. That is what makes LISTEN/NOTIFY safe to use with transactions, unlike calling an email API directly from the code path that may still roll back.

sql-advanced:4.prompt: A nightly UPDATE touches 1M rows of accounts, and a FOR EACH ROW AFTER UPDATE trigger inserts one audit row per change. The job is slow. Which PostgreSQL feature lets you audit the whole statement in one set-based insert?
options: A FOR EACH STATEMENT trigger using transition tables (REFERENCING OLD TABLE AS o NEW TABLE AS n)
Turning the trigger into a BEFORE trigger
Adding a WHEN (pg_trigger_depth() = 0) clause
Using a rule instead of a trigger
sql-advanced:4.explanation: Statement-level triggers with transition tables (PostgreSQL 10+) fire once and can see all changed rows as tables, so one INSERT ... SELECT replaces 1M separate inserts. Switching to BEFORE still fires once per row.

sql-advanced:4.prompt: Which are good reasons NOT to put a piece of logic in a trigger? Select all that apply.
options: It needs to call an external service
It changes often and the team tests logic in application code
Developers routinely forget that the trigger exists when debugging writes
It must write an audit record atomically with every change
It sets updated_at = now() on every update
sql-advanced:4.explanation: External calls cannot be rolled back with the transaction, fast-changing rules belong where they are tested, and hidden behaviour hurts debugging. Atomic audit rows and updated_at maintenance are standard, low-risk trigger uses.

sql-advanced:4.prompt: Which statements about PostgreSQL triggers are true? Select all that apply.
options: Row-level ON DELETE triggers do not fire for TRUNCATE
A trigger's changes are part of the same transaction as the statement that fired it
An AFTER ROW trigger can modify NEW to change what is stored
A trigger's own writes can fire other triggers, including cascading ones
sql-advanced:4.explanation: TRUNCATE only fires statement-level ON TRUNCATE triggers. Trigger work commits or rolls back with the statement and can cascade into other triggers. Only BEFORE row triggers can modify NEW; by AFTER time the row is already written.

sql-advanced:4.prompt: In PostgreSQL, a function called from a SELECT can run COMMIT to persist its work early.
options: True
False
sql-advanced:4.explanation: Functions run inside the calling statement's transaction and cannot commit; PostgreSQL raises an error on COMMIT there. Only procedures invoked with CALL (outside an explicit transaction block) can control transactions.

sql-advanced:4.prompt: A BEFORE UPDATE FOR EACH ROW trigger in PostgreSQL can change values in NEW, and the modified values are what get stored.
options: True
False
sql-advanced:4.explanation: BEFORE row triggers return the row to store, so assigning NEW.updated_at := now() and returning NEW is the standard updated_at pattern. AFTER triggers see the final row but cannot change it.

sql-advanced:5.prompt: In PostgreSQL, which query returns the median salary (interpolated if the count is even)?
options: SELECT percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary) FROM employees
SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees
SELECT salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary LIMIT 1 OFFSET (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees) / 2
SELECT MODE() WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary) FROM employees
sql-advanced:5.explanation: percentile_cont(0.5) is the ordered-set aggregate for the median and interpolates between the two middle values. AVG is the mean, mode() is the most frequent value, and the OFFSET trick returns only one of the two middle rows when the count is even.

sql-advanced:5.prompt: Salaries are 100, 100, 90, 80. Which query returns 80 as the 3rd highest distinct salary?
options: Filter ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) = 3
Filter RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) = 3
Filter DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) = 3
SELECT salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 2
sql-advanced:5.explanation: DENSE_RANK assigns 1, 1, 2, 3, so rank 3 is 80. ROW_NUMBER (1, 2, 3, 4) and RANK (1, 1, 3, 4) both put 90 in position 3, and the OFFSET query without DISTINCT also returns 90.

sql-advanced:5.prompt: Which query lists email addresses that appear more than once in users?
options: SELECT email FROM users WHERE COUNT(*) > 1 GROUP BY email
SELECT email FROM users GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
SELECT DISTINCT email FROM users
SELECT email, COUNT(*) OVER () FROM users WHERE COUNT(*) > 1
sql-advanced:5.explanation: Group by email, then filter the groups with HAVING. Aggregates are not allowed in WHERE, and DISTINCT returns every email, not just duplicates.

sql-advanced:5.prompt: In PostgreSQL, which statement deletes duplicate users by email, keeping the row with the smallest id?
options: DELETE FROM users a USING users b WHERE a.email = b.email AND a.id > b.id
DELETE FROM users a USING users b WHERE a.email = b.email AND a.id < b.id
DELETE FROM users WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT MAX(id) FROM users GROUP BY email)
DELETE FROM users a USING users b WHERE a.email = b.email
sql-advanced:5.explanation: A row is deleted if another row with the same email has a smaller id, so only the minimum id survives. a.id < b.id keeps the largest id, the NOT IN version also keeps the max, and the last option deletes every row whose email matches any row, including itself.

sql-advanced:5.prompt: You need the top earner(s) in each department, showing every employee tied for first. Which approach is correct?
options: DISTINCT ON (dept_id) ... ORDER BY dept_id, salary DESC
Filter RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) = 1
Filter ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) = 1
GROUP BY dept_id and SELECT MAX(salary), name
sql-advanced:5.explanation: RANK gives every tied top salary rank 1, so ties are kept. DISTINCT ON and ROW_NUMBER pick exactly one row per department, and selecting name next to MAX without grouping by it is an error in PostgreSQL.

sql-advanced:5.prompt: For a login streaks report, why does subtracting the row number from each date identify runs of consecutive days?
options: ROW_NUMBER skips numbers on missing days, keeping grp constant
Within a consecutive run both day and row number increase by 1 per row, so their difference is constant; a gap shifts it to a new value
Subtracting integers from dates resets at month boundaries, which separates the runs
grp is the length of the streak so far
sql-advanced:5.explanation: This is the gaps-and-islands trick: consecutive dates and consecutive row numbers move together, so day - rn stays the same within a run and jumps after a gap. GROUP BY user_id, grp then gives each streak's start, end and length. ROW_NUMBER never skips numbers.

sql-advanced:5.prompt: employees(id, name, salary, manager_id). Which query lists employees who earn more than their manager?
options: SELECT e.name FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id WHERE e.salary > m.salary
SELECT e.name FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.id = m.manager_id WHERE e.salary > m.salary
SELECT name FROM employees WHERE salary > (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees)
SELECT e.name FROM employees e WHERE e.salary > e.manager_id
sql-advanced:5.explanation: Join each employee to their manager row (e.manager_id = m.id) and compare salaries. The reversed join compares managers with their reports, and comparing salary to manager_id compares money with an id.

sql-advanced:5.prompt: Which queries correctly return the 2nd highest distinct salary (returning NULL or no row when it does not exist is acceptable)? Select all that apply.
options: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees)
SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1
SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM (SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS r FROM employees) t WHERE r = 2
SELECT salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1
sql-advanced:5.explanation: All three correct forms de-duplicate salaries before picking the second one. The last query skips one row, not one distinct value, so when two people share the top salary it returns the top salary again.

sql-advanced:5.prompt: orders.customer_id is nullable and contains some NULLs. Which queries correctly return customer ids that have no orders? Select all that apply.
options: SELECT c.id FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)
SELECT c.id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL
SELECT id FROM customers WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)
SELECT id FROM customers EXCEPT SELECT customer_id FROM orders
sql-advanced:5.explanation: NOT EXISTS, the LEFT JOIN anti-join and EXCEPT all handle NULLs correctly (a NULL from orders cannot remove a real id from EXCEPT). NOT IN returns nothing once the subquery contains a NULL, because every comparison becomes unknown.

sql-advanced:5.prompt: For a "top 3 products per category by revenue" query, filtering RANK() <= 3 can return more than 3 rows for a category.
options: True
False
sql-advanced:5.explanation: Ties share a rank: revenues 50, 40, 40, 40 rank 1, 2, 2, 2, so four rows pass RANK() <= 3. Use ROW_NUMBER (with a tiebreaker) if exactly 3 rows are required.

sql-advanced:5.prompt: If every employee earns the same salary, SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees) returns zero rows.
options: True
False
sql-advanced:5.explanation: An aggregate without GROUP BY always returns one row; no rows match the WHERE, so MAX is NULL and you get one row containing NULL. The LIMIT/OFFSET variant is the one that returns zero rows.
